Where it began

Cameron Green was born on 3 June 1999 in Subiaco, the Perth suburb where he grew up. He joined the local Subiaco-Floreat club as a boy of ten, starting in the under-13s, and moved up so fast that he was playing first grade at 16.

He came into the Western Australia side as a bowler who could bat. On his first-class debut, in February 2017, he took five wickets in an innings, and nobody had done that in the Sheffield Shield at a younger age. Later he set about his batting in earnest, and in 2021 he made 251 against Queensland.

The player

Green's Test debut came against India in December 2020. By November 2026 he had played 39 Tests, making 1,920 runs at 34.29 with three hundreds, and taking 39 wickets with a best of 5 for 27, which came in the Boxing Day Test at Melbourne in 2022. He had also held 41 catches.

His first Test hundred, 114, came in Ahmedabad in 2023, and that year he was part of the Australian sides that won both the World Test Championship final and the World Cup. In early 2024, given a new job at number four, he made 174 not out at the Basin Reserve against New Zealand, adding 116 for the last wicket with Josh Hazlewood. In August 2026 he made his first Test hundred in Australia, against Bangladesh.

What made him special

Few cricketers are asked to do quite so much. Green could take the new ball at a lively pace, then come in at number four and play the long innings the side needed. His 174 not out, on a pitch that helped the seamers, showed how calm he could be while wickets fell at the other end.

What he had to learn was patience with the bat. His runs often came in bursts rather than a steady stream, and for a while the Test selectors looked elsewhere. He answered the way all-rounders like best, by going away and making more runs.

Away from the middle

Green was much in demand in franchise cricket. He played the Big Bash for Perth Scorchers and moved through three IPL sides: Mumbai, Bangalore and, for 2026, Kolkata. In 2025 he spent the start of the English summer with Gloucestershire and made three hundreds in a handful of county games.

And finally

Green began as a bowler who batted, then turned himself into a batter who bowls. If he keeps going this way, Western Australia may one day ask him to keep wicket as well, just to see what happens.
